questions.q: An electric dipole consists of two equal and opposite charges separated by a very small distance $2a$. The electric potential $V$ at a point located at a distance $r$ from the center of the dipole, such that $r \gg 2a$, varies with $r$ as:
questions.solution:
For a short electric dipole, the electric potential $V$ at a distance $r$ from its center is given by $V = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0} \dfrac{p \cos\theta}{r^2}$.

Since $r \gg 2a$, the potential $V$ is inversely proportional to the square of the distance.

Therefore, $V \propto \dfrac{1}{r^2}$.

Answer: $\dfrac{1}{r^2}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
Match List-I with List-II for a uniformly charged thin spherical shell of radius $R$ and total charge $Q$ (where $k = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}$ and $r$ is the distance from the centre of the shell).

List-IList-II
A. Electric field at $r = R/2$I. Zero
B. Electric potential at $r = R/2$II. $\dfrac{kQ}{R}$
C. Electric field at $r = 2R$III. $\dfrac{kQ}{4R^2}$
D. Electric potential at $r = 2R$IV. $\dfrac{kQ}{2R}$

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.solution:
For a uniformly charged thin spherical shell of radius $R$ and charge $Q$:

Inside the shell ($r \lt R$):
The electric field is zero everywhere. At $r = R/2$, $E = 0$. (A matches I)
The electric potential is constant and equal to the potential at the surface. At $r = R/2$, $V = \dfrac{kQ}{R}$. (B matches II)

Outside the shell ($r \gt R$):
The shell behaves as a point charge located at its centre.
The electric field at $r = 2R$ is $E = \dfrac{kQ}{(2R)^2} = \dfrac{kQ}{4R^2}$. (C matches III)
The electric potential at $r = 2R$ is $V = \dfrac{kQ}{2R}$. (D matches IV)

Therefore, the correct matching is A-I, B-II, C-III, D-IV.

Answer: A-I, B-II, C-III, D-IV

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A positively charged thin metallic shell of radius $R$ is placed in a vacuum. Which of the following correctly describes the variation of the magnitude of the electric field $E$ with radial distance $r$ from the centre of the shell?
options: $E$ is constant and non-zero for $r \lt  R$, and decreases proportionally to $\dfrac{1}{r}$ for $r \gt  R$.
$E$ increases linearly with $r$ for $r \lt  R$, and decreases proportionally to $\dfrac{1}{r^2}$ for $r \gt  R$.
$E$ is zero for $r \lt  R$, and decreases proportionally to $\dfrac{1}{r^2}$ for $r \gt  R$.
$E$ is zero for $r \lt  R$, and decreases proportionally to $\dfrac{1}{r}$ for $r \gt  R$.
questions.solution:
For a uniformly charged thin metallic shell of radius $R$ carrying a total charge $Q$:

Inside the conducting shell ($r \lt R$), the electric field is exactly zero because all the charge resides on the outer surface and there is no enclosed charge ($E = 0$).

Outside the shell ($r \gt R$), the shell behaves as if its entire charge is concentrated at the centre. By Gauss's law, the electric field is given by $E = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0} \dfrac{Q}{r^2}$. Thus, the electric field decreases proportionally to $\dfrac{1}{r^2}$.

Therefore, $E$ is zero for $r \lt R$ and decreases as $\dfrac{1}{r^2}$ for $r \gt R$.

Answer: $E$ is zero for $r \lt R$, and decreases proportionally to $\dfrac{1}{r^2}$ for $r \gt R$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: An electric dipole consisting of two opposite charges of magnitude $4 \mu\text{C}$ separated by a distance of $5 \text{ mm}$ is placed in a uniform electric field of $10^5 \text{ N C}^{-1}$. If the dipole experiences a torque of $10^{-3} \text{ N m}$, what is the angle between the dipole moment and the electric field?
questions.solution:
The electric dipole moment $p$ is given by the product of the charge magnitude and the separation distance:

$p = q \times d$
$p = (4 \times 10^{-6} \text{ C}) \times (5 \times 10^{-3} \text{ m})$
$p = 20 \times 10^{-9} \text{ C m} = 2 \times 10^{-8} \text{ C m}$

The torque $\tau$ experienced by the dipole in a uniform electric field is:

$\tau = pE \sin \theta$

Substituting the given values:

$10^{-3} = (2 \times 10^{-8}) \times (10^5) \times \sin \theta$
$10^{-3} = 2 \times 10^{-3} \sin \theta$
$\sin \theta = \dfrac{1}{2}$

Therefore, the angle $\theta$ is $30^\circ$.

Answer: $30^\circ$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
A solid conducting sphere of radius $10\text{ cm}$ is given a total charge of $2\mu\text{C}$. What is the electric potential at a point located $5\text{ cm}$ from the centre of the sphere?

(Take $\dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} = 9 \times 10^9\text{ N m}^2\text{ C}^{-2}$)
questions.solution:
For a solid conducting sphere, all the given charge resides on its outer surface. Electrostatically, it behaves exactly like a thin spherical shell.

The electric field inside the conducting sphere is zero, which means the electric potential is constant everywhere inside the sphere and is equal to the potential on its surface.

Therefore, the potential at $r = 5\text{ cm}$ (which is inside the sphere) is determined by the radius of the sphere $R$, not the internal distance $r$:
$V = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \dfrac{Q}{R}$

Substituting the given values ($R = 10\text{ cm} = 0.1\text{ m}$, $Q = 2 \times 10^{-6}\text{ C}$):
$V = \dfrac{9 \times 10^9 \times 2 \times 10^{-6}}{0.1}$
$V = 1.8 \times 10^5\text{ V}$

Answer: $1.8 \times 10^5\text{ V}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: An electric dipole of length $2a$ is placed with its center at the origin. Let $A$ and $B$ be two points on the axial line at distances $2a$ and $3a$ respectively from the center of the dipole, both on the side of the positive charge. The ratio of the electric potential at point $A$ to the electric potential at point $B$ is:
questions.solution:
The electric potential $V$ at a distance $r$ from the center of a finite dipole of length $2a$ on its axial line (closer to the positive charge) is given by the exact formula:
$V = \dfrac{Kp}{r^2 - a^2}$

For point $A$, the distance from the center is $r_A = 2a$. The potential at $A$ is:
$V_A = \dfrac{Kp}{(2a)^2 - a^2} = \dfrac{Kp}{4a^2 - a^2} = \dfrac{Kp}{3a^2}$

For point $B$, the distance from the center is $r_B = 3a$. The potential at $B$ is:
$V_B = \dfrac{Kp}{(3a)^2 - a^2} = \dfrac{Kp}{9a^2 - a^2} = \dfrac{Kp}{8a^2}$

The ratio of the potentials is:
$\dfrac{V_A}{V_B} = \dfrac{\dfrac{Kp}{3a^2}}{\dfrac{Kp}{8a^2}} = \dfrac{8}{3}$

Thus, the ratio is $8:3$.

(Note: Using the short dipole approximation $V \propto \dfrac{1}{r^2}$ would incorrectly yield $9:4$.)

Answer: $8:3$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A solid non-conducting sphere of radius $R$ has a total charge $Q$ distributed uniformly throughout its volume. The magnitude of the potential difference between the centre of the sphere and a point on its surface is:
questions.solution:
For a uniformly charged solid non-conducting sphere, the electric potential at a distance $r$ from the centre (where $r \leq R$) is given by:
$V(r) = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \dfrac{Q(3R^2 - r^2)}{2R^3}$

At the centre of the sphere ($r = 0$), the potential is:
$V_{\text{centre}} = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \dfrac{3Q}{2R}$

At the surface of the sphere ($r = R$), the potential is:
$V_{\text{surface}} = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \dfrac{Q(3R^2 - R^2)}{2R^3} = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \dfrac{Q}{R}$

The magnitude of the potential difference between the centre and the surface is:
$\Delta V = V_{\text{centre}} - V_{\text{surface}}$
$\Delta V = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \left( \dfrac{3Q}{2R} - \dfrac{Q}{R} \right)$
$\Delta V = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \dfrac{Q}{2R}$

Answer: $\dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \dfrac{Q}{2R}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
An electric dipole consists of two charges $+q$ and $-q$ separated by a distance of $2\text{ cm}$. What is the work done by an external agent in moving a test charge $+Q$ slowly from a point on the equatorial plane (at a distance of $5\text{ cm}$ from the center of the dipole) to a point on the axial line at a distance of $3\text{ cm}$ from the center (on the side of the positive charge)?

(Take $K = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}$)
questions.solution:
The work done by an external agent in moving a charge $+Q$ is given by $W = Q(V_f - V_i)$, where $V_i$ and $V_f$ are the initial and final electric potentials respectively.

The initial point is on the equatorial plane of the dipole. The electric potential at any point on the equatorial plane of a dipole is zero, so $V_i = 0$.

The final point is on the axial line at a distance $r = 3\text{ cm}$ from the center, on the side of the positive charge. The length of the dipole is $2a = 2\text{ cm}$, so $a = 1\text{ cm}$.

The exact electric potential at an axial point is:
$V_f = \dfrac{Kq}{r-a} - \dfrac{Kq}{r+a}$

Substituting the given values (in meters):
$V_f = \dfrac{Kq}{(3 - 1) \times 10^{-2}} - \dfrac{Kq}{(3 + 1) \times 10^{-2}}$
$V_f = \dfrac{Kq}{2 \times 10^{-2}} - \dfrac{Kq}{4 \times 10^{-2}}$
$V_f = Kq \times 10^2 \left(\dfrac{1}{2} - \dfrac{1}{4}\right) = Kq \times 100 \times \dfrac{1}{4} = 25 Kq$

Therefore, the work done is:
$W = Q(25 Kq - 0) = 25 KqQ$

Answer: $25 KqQ$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: An uncharged solid metallic sphere is placed in a uniform external electric field. Which of the following statements correctly describes the electric field lines just outside its surface and the electrostatic potential inside the sphere?
options: Electric field lines pass straight through the sphere parallel to each other, and the potential inside is zero.
Electric field lines are tangential to the surface, and the potential inside is constant but non-zero.
Electric field lines are normal to the surface, and the potential inside is strictly zero.
Electric field lines are normal to the surface, and the potential inside is constant and equal to the surface potential.
questions.solution:
In electrostatics, the entire volume and surface of a metallic conductor are at the same electrostatic potential. Thus, a conductor in electrostatic equilibrium forms an equipotential volume, and its surface is an equipotential surface.

Because the surface is an equipotential surface, the external electric field lines must be exactly normal (perpendicular) to the surface at every point. If they were not normal, there would be a tangential component of the electric field along the surface, which would cause charges to flow, violating the condition of electrostatic equilibrium.

Inside the conductor, the electric field is zero. The relation $E = -\dfrac{dV}{dr} = 0$ implies that the potential $V$ is constant throughout the volume of the conductor and is exactly equal to its value on the surface.

Therefore, the electric field lines are normal to the surface, and the potential inside is constant and equal to the surface potential.

Answer: Electric field lines are normal to the surface, and the potential inside is constant and equal to the surface potential.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
Match the physical quantities for a charged conducting sphere of radius $R$ having a uniform surface charge density $\sigma$ (List-I) with their corresponding expressions (List-II).

List-IList-II
(A) Electric field inside ($r \lt R$)(I) $\dfrac{\sigma R^2}{\varepsilon_0 r}$
(B) Electric potential inside ($r \lt R$)(II) $0$
(C) Electric field outside ($r \gt R$)(III) $\dfrac{\sigma R}{\varepsilon_0}$
(D) Electric potential outside ($r \gt R$)(IV) $\dfrac{\sigma R^2}{\varepsilon_0 r^2}$

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.solution:
For a conducting sphere of radius $R$ with uniform surface charge density $\sigma$, the total charge is $q = \sigma(4\pi R^2)$.

(A) Inside the conductor ($r \lt R$), the electric field is zero. So, (A) matches (II).

(B) The electric potential inside the conductor is constant and equal to the potential at its surface: $V = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{q}{R} = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{\sigma(4\pi R^2)}{R} = \dfrac{\sigma R}{\varepsilon_0}$. So, (B) matches (III).

(C) The electric field outside the sphere ($r \gt R$) is $E = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{q}{r^2} = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{\sigma(4\pi R^2)}{r^2} = \dfrac{\sigma R^2}{\varepsilon_0 r^2}$. So, (C) matches (IV).

(D) The electric potential outside the sphere ($r \gt R$) is $V = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{q}{r} = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{\sigma(4\pi R^2)}{r} = \dfrac{\sigma R^2}{\varepsilon_0 r}$. So, (D) matches (I).

Therefore, the correct matching is (A)-(II), (B)-(III), (C)-(IV), (D)-(I).

Answer: (A)-(II), (B)-(III), (C)-(IV), (D)-(I)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): If a solid spherical conductor of radius $R$ is given a charge $Q$, the magnitude of the electric field at a distance $x$ ($x \gt 0$) from its surface is $\dfrac{Q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0(R+x)^2}$.

Reason (R): For calculating the electric field at an external point, the effective distance is measured from the surface of the charged spherical conductor.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
options: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are correct and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are correct but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Assertion (A) is correct but Reason (R) is incorrect.
Assertion (A) is incorrect but Reason (R) is correct.
questions.solution:
The electric field at an external point due to a charged spherical conductor is calculated by assuming its entire charge is concentrated at its geometric centre.

If a point is at a distance $x$ from the surface of a sphere of radius $R$, its distance from the centre of the sphere is $r = R + x$.

The electric field is $E = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{Q}{r^2} = \dfrac{Q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0(R+x)^2}$. Thus, the Assertion is correct.

The Reason is incorrect because the effective distance for an external point is measured from the centre of the sphere, not from its surface.

Answer: Assertion (A) is correct but Reason (R) is incorrect.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: An uncharged solid spherical conductor of radius $R$ has an off-center cavity. A point charge $+Q$ is placed inside the cavity. The outer surface of the conductor is then connected to the earth. What is the net charge on the conductor and the magnitude of the electric field at a distance $r$ ($r \gt  R$) from the center of the sphere?
questions.solution:
When a point charge $+Q$ is placed inside the cavity, it induces a charge $-Q$ on the inner surface of the cavity and a charge $+Q$ on the outer surface of the conductor.

When the outer surface of the conductor is earthed, its potential becomes zero. The induced charge $+Q$ on the outer surface flows to the earth. However, the induced charge $-Q$ on the inner surface remains bound due to the electrostatic attraction of the $+Q$ charge inside the cavity. This is necessary to maintain a zero electric field inside the bulk of the conductor.

Therefore, the net charge remaining on the conductor is $-Q$.

Since there is no charge on the outer surface of the spherical conductor, the electric field at any point outside the conductor ($r \gt R$) is zero.

Answer: $-Q$ and Zero

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A point charge $Q$ is placed at a distance $r$ on the axial line of a short electric dipole. The electrostatic force experienced by the charge is $F$. If the distance of the point charge from the center of the dipole is doubled to $2r$, the new force experienced by it will be:
questions.solution:
The electric field $E$ on the axial line of a short electric dipole at a distance $r$ from its center is given by $E = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0} \dfrac{2p}{r^3}$.

The force experienced by the point charge $Q$ is $F = QE$. Thus, $F \propto \dfrac{1}{r^3}$.

When the distance is doubled ($r' = 2r$), the new force $F'$ becomes:

$F' \propto \dfrac{1}{(2r)^3} = \dfrac{1}{8r^3}$

Therefore, $F' = \dfrac{F}{8}$.

Answer: $\dfrac{F}{8}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): For an isolated uncharged solid conducting sphere with an off-center cavity containing a point charge $q$, the magnitude of the electric field at a point outside the sphere is greater on the side closer to the cavity.

Reason (R): The induced charge on the outer surface of the sphere distributes uniformly, perfectly shielding the outside region from the asymmetry of the internal cavity.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
options: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are correct but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A)
questions.solution:
The Assertion is incorrect. For an isolated uncharged solid conducting sphere with a cavity containing a point charge $q$, the electric field outside the sphere depends only on the charge distribution on its outer surface. It does not depend on the position of the cavity or the charge inside it.

The Reason is correct. The point charge $q$ induces a charge $-q$ on the inner surface of the cavity and a charge $+q$ on the outer surface of the sphere. Because the outer surface is perfectly spherical and there are no external electric fields, this induced charge $+q$ distributes itself uniformly. This uniform distribution creates a spherically symmetric electric field outside the conductor, effectively shielding the outside region from any asymmetry of the internal cavity.

Therefore, the electric field outside is uniform in all radial directions, making the Assertion incorrect.

Answer: (A) is incorrect but (R) is correct

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): An electric dipole placed antiparallel to a non-uniform electric field experiences a net force towards the region of weaker electric field.
Reason (R): The net torque on an electric dipole is zero when it is placed antiparallel to an electric field.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
options: Both Assertion and Reason are true and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion.
Assertion is true but Reason is false.
Assertion is false but Reason is true.
questions.solution:
Assertion (A) is true: When an electric dipole is placed antiparallel to a non-uniform electric field, its dipole moment $\vec{p}$ is opposite to the electric field $\vec{E}$. In this orientation, the negative charge of the dipole is located in the region of stronger electric field, while the positive charge is in the weaker field region. The force on the negative charge (opposite to $\vec{E}$) dominates, resulting in a net force that pushes the dipole towards the weaker electric field region.

Reason (R) is true: The torque on a dipole is given by $\vec{\tau} = \vec{p} \times \vec{E}$. When the dipole is antiparallel to the field, the angle between $\vec{p}$ and $\vec{E}$ is $180^{\circ}$, so $\sin(180^{\circ}) = 0$, and the net torque is zero.

However, Reason (R) does not explain Assertion (A). The correct explanation for (A) is that the net force depends on the difference in field strength at the locations of the two charges. Therefore, both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

Answer: Both Assertion and Reason are true but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: An uncharged solid conducting sphere of radius $R$ has an off-center spherical cavity. A point charge $+q$ is placed inside the cavity at a distance $x$ from the center of the solid sphere. What is the electric potential of the solid conductor? (Assume the potential at infinity is zero, and $k = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}$)
options: Cannot be determined from the given information
questions.solution:
The electric potential of a conductor in electrostatic equilibrium is constant throughout its volume and on its surface.

When a point charge $+q$ is placed inside the cavity, it induces a charge $-q$ on the inner surface of the cavity and a charge $+q$ on the outer surface of the sphere.

By the principle of electrostatic shielding, the electric field produced by the point charge $+q$ and the induced charge $-q$ on the inner surface is completely confined within the cavity. Their combined contribution to the electric potential at any point in the bulk of the conductor or on its outer surface is zero.

Therefore, the potential of the conductor is determined entirely by the induced charge $+q$ on its outer surface. Since the outer surface is spherical with radius $R$, this charge distributes uniformly.

The electric potential at the surface (and thus throughout the entire conductor) is simply the potential due to this uniformly distributed outer charge, which is $V = \dfrac{kq}{R}$.

Answer: $\dfrac{kq}{R}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A conducting sphere of radius $R$ carries a total charge $Q$. It is connected by a thin conducting wire to an initially uncharged conducting sphere of radius $3R$. After electrostatic equilibrium is reached, what is the surface charge density of the smaller sphere?
questions.solution:
Let the final charges on the smaller and larger spheres be $q_1$ and $q_2$ respectively.

When connected by a wire, their potentials become equal: $V_1 = V_2$.

$\dfrac{k q_1}{R} = \dfrac{k q_2}{3R} \Rightarrow q_2 = 3q_1$

By conservation of charge, the total charge remains $Q$:
$q_1 + q_2 = Q$
$q_1 + 3q_1 = Q \Rightarrow 4q_1 = Q \Rightarrow q_1 = \dfrac{Q}{4}$

The surface charge density of the smaller sphere is:
$\sigma_1 = \dfrac{q_1}{4\pi R^2} = \dfrac{\dfrac{Q}{4}}{4\pi R^2} = \dfrac{Q}{16\pi R^2}$

Answer: $\dfrac{Q}{16\pi R^2}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Sixty-four identical spherical liquid drops, each carrying the same charge, coalesce to form a single large drop. What is the ratio of the total initial electrostatic energy of all the small drops to the final electrostatic energy of the large drop?
questions.solution:
Let the charge on each small drop be $q$ and its radius be $r$. The electrostatic energy of one small drop is $U_{\text{small}} = \dfrac{kq^2}{2r}$.

For $N = 64$ such drops, the total initial energy is:
$U_i = N \times U_{\text{small}} = 64 \times \dfrac{kq^2}{2r}$

When they coalesce, the total charge of the large drop is $Q = Nq = 64q$.
By conservation of volume, the radius $R$ of the large drop is:
$\dfrac{4}{3}\pi R^3 = 64 \times \dfrac{4}{3}\pi r^3 \Rightarrow R = 64^{1/3}r = 4r$

The final electrostatic energy of the large drop is:
$U_f = \dfrac{kQ^2}{2R} = \dfrac{k(64q)^2}{2(4r)} = \dfrac{4096}{4} \times \dfrac{kq^2}{2r} = 1024 \times \dfrac{kq^2}{2r}$

The ratio of total initial energy to final energy is:
$\dfrac{U_i}{U_f} = \dfrac{64}{1024} = \dfrac{1}{16}$

Thus, the required ratio is $1:16$.

Answer: $1:16$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
Match the configurations of an electric dipole in List-I with their corresponding mechanical states in List-II.

List-IList-II
(A) Dipole parallel to a unidirectional non-uniform electric field(I) Net force is zero, torque is zero, stable equilibrium
(B) Dipole antiparallel to a unidirectional non-uniform electric field(II) Net force is non-zero, torque is zero, stable equilibrium
(C) Dipole perpendicular to a uniform electric field(III) Net force is zero, torque is non-zero
(D) Dipole parallel to a uniform electric field(IV) Net force is non-zero, torque is zero, unstable equilibrium

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.solution:
In a uniform electric field, the net force on a dipole is always zero. If the dipole is parallel to the field ($\theta = 0^\circ$), the torque is zero and it is in stable equilibrium. If it is perpendicular ($\theta = 90^\circ$), the torque is maximum and non-zero.

In a non-uniform electric field, the net force is generally non-zero. If the dipole is parallel to the field ($\theta = 0^\circ$), the torque is zero and it is in stable equilibrium. If it is antiparallel ($\theta = 180^\circ$), the torque is zero and it is in unstable equilibrium.

Matching these conditions:
(A) Parallel to non-uniform field: Net force non-zero, torque zero, stable equilibrium (II).
(B) Antiparallel to non-uniform field: Net force non-zero, torque zero, unstable equilibrium (IV).
(C) Perpendicular to uniform field: Net force zero, torque non-zero (III).
(D) Parallel to uniform field: Net force zero, torque zero, stable equilibrium (I).

Answer: (A)-(II), (B)-(IV), (C)-(III), (D)-(I)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: An uncharged solid spherical conductor contains a cavity within it. A point charge $+Q$ is placed inside the cavity without touching its walls. What will be the induced charges on the inner surface of the cavity and the outer surface of the conductor, respectively?
questions.solution:
Consider a Gaussian surface entirely within the solid material of the conductor, enclosing the cavity. In electrostatic equilibrium, the electric field inside the conducting material is zero everywhere.

According to Gauss's law, the net flux through this surface is zero, which means the net charge enclosed must be zero. Therefore, an induced charge of $-Q$ must appear on the inner surface of the cavity to exactly cancel the $+Q$ point charge inside.

Since the conductor is initially uncharged and isolated, its total charge must remain zero. By conservation of charge, the sum of the charges on the inner and outer surfaces must be zero. Thus, a charge of $+Q$ must appear on the outer surface of the conductor.

Answer: $-Q$ and $+Q$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
Match the electrostatic configurations involving infinitely long straight wires with uniform linear charge density $\lambda$ in List-I with the magnitude of the net electric field at the specified point in List-II.

List-IList-II
(A) Midpoint between two parallel wires with charge densities $+\lambda$ and $+\lambda$ separated by a distance $2R$(I) Zero
(B) Midpoint between two parallel wires with charge densities $+\lambda$ and $-\lambda$ separated by a distance $2R$(II) $\dfrac{\lambda}{\pi\epsilon_0 R}$
(C) A point at a perpendicular distance $R$ from a single wire with charge density $+\lambda$(III) $\dfrac{\lambda}{2\pi\epsilon_0 R}$
(D) A point at a perpendicular distance $2R$ from a single wire with charge density $+\lambda$(IV) $\dfrac{\lambda}{4\pi\epsilon_0 R}$


Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.solution:
For A: The electric fields due to the two identical wires at the midpoint are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction. Net electric field is zero. (A matches I)

For B: The electric fields due to the two wires at the midpoint are in the same direction. Net electric field $E = \dfrac{\lambda}{2\pi\epsilon_0 R} + \dfrac{\lambda}{2\pi\epsilon_0 R} = \dfrac{\lambda}{\pi\epsilon_0 R}$. (B matches II)

For C: The electric field at a distance $R$ from a single infinite line charge is $E = \dfrac{\lambda}{2\pi\epsilon_0 R}$. (C matches III)

For D: The electric field at a distance $2R$ from a single infinite line charge is $E = \dfrac{\lambda}{2\pi\epsilon_0 (2R)} = \dfrac{\lambda}{4\pi\epsilon_0 R}$. (D matches IV)

Answer: (A) → (I), (B) → (II), (C) → (III), (D) → (IV)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A charged conducting sphere has a radius $R$. The electric field at a distance $x$ ($x \gt  R$) from the centre of the sphere is $E$. What is the electric potential at a distance $y$ ($y \lt  R$) from the centre of the sphere?
questions.solution:
For a point outside the charged conducting sphere ($x \gt R$), the electric field is given by:
$E = \dfrac{k q}{x^{2}}$
$\Rightarrow k q = E x^{2}$

For any point inside the conducting sphere ($y \lt R$), the electric potential is constant and equal to the potential at its surface.
$V = \dfrac{k q}{R}$

Substituting the value of $k q$ from the first equation:
$V = \dfrac{E x^{2}}{R}$

Answer: $\dfrac{E x^{2}}{R}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A large spherical liquid drop is charged to a potential of $500\text{ V}$. It breaks up into $N$ identical smaller spherical drops. If the potential of each of the smaller drops is found to be $20\text{ V}$, what is the value of $N$?
questions.solution:
Let the radius of the large drop be $R$ and its charge be $Q$. Its potential is given by $V_{\text{large}} = \dfrac{kQ}{R}$.

When it breaks into $N$ identical smaller drops of radius $r$ and charge $q$, the total charge and total volume are conserved.
Charge conservation: $Q = Nq$
Volume conservation: $\dfrac{4}{3}\pi R^3 = N \times \dfrac{4}{3}\pi r^3 \Rightarrow R = N^{1/3}r$

The potential of each small drop is $V_{\text{small}} = \dfrac{kq}{r}$.

Taking the ratio of the potentials:
$\dfrac{V_{\text{large}}}{V_{\text{small}}} = \dfrac{\dfrac{kQ}{R}}{\dfrac{kq}{r}} = \left(\dfrac{Q}{q}\right)\left(\dfrac{r}{R}\right) = (N)\left(\dfrac{1}{N^{1/3}}\right) = N^{2/3}$

Given $V_{\text{large}} = 500\text{ V}$ and $V_{\text{small}} = 20\text{ V}$:
$N^{2/3} = \dfrac{500}{20} = 25$

Solving for $N$:
$N = (25)^{3/2} = (5^2)^{3/2} = 5^3 = 125$

Answer: $125$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
A uniformly charged spherical conductor of radius $10\text{ cm}$ has a total charge of $4 \times 10^{-6}\text{ C}$. The magnitude of the electric field produced by this charge distribution at a certain point outside the sphere is $9 \times 10^{5}\text{ N C}^{-1}$. What is the distance of this point from the centre of the sphere?
$\left(\dfrac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} = 9 \times 10^9\text{ N m}^2\text{ C}^{-2}\right)$
questions.solution:
The electric field outside a uniformly charged spherical conductor at a distance $r$ from its centre is given by:

$E = \dfrac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} \dfrac{Q}{r^2}$

Rearranging for $r^2$:

$r^2 = \dfrac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} \dfrac{Q}{E}$

Substituting the given values:

$r^2 = \dfrac{9 \times 10^9 \times 4 \times 10^{-6}}{9 \times 10^5}$

$r^2 = \dfrac{36 \times 10^3}{9 \times 10^5} = 4 \times 10^{-2}\text{ m}^2$

Taking the square root:

$r = 0.2\text{ m} = 20\text{ cm}$

Answer: $20\text{ cm}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Which of the following correctly describes the variation of the magnitude of the electric field $E$ with distance $r$ from the center of a uniformly charged hollow metallic sphere of radius $R$?
options: $E$ is zero for $r \lt  R$, abruptly becomes maximum at $r = R$, and then decreases proportionally to $1/r^{2}$ for $r \gt  R$.
$E$ increases linearly with $r$ for $r \lt  R$, and decreases proportionally to $1/r^{2}$ for $r \gt  R$.
$E$ is constant and non-zero for $r \lt  R$, and decreases proportionally to $1/r^{2}$ for $r \gt  R$.
questions.solution:
Inside a hollow metallic sphere, the charge resides entirely on the outer surface. Therefore, the electric field inside the sphere is zero ($E = 0$ for $r \lt R$).

Outside the sphere, the charge distribution behaves as if its entire charge is concentrated at the center. The electric field follows an inverse-square law, $E \propto 1/r^{2}$ for $r \gt R$.

At the surface ($r = R$), the electric field is maximum. Thus, the field is zero inside, jumps to a maximum at the surface, and then decreases as $1/r^{2}$ outside.

Answer: $E$ is zero for $r \lt R$, abruptly becomes maximum at $r = R$, and then decreases proportionally to $1/r^{2}$ for $r \gt R$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two concentric thin metallic shells A and B have radii $R$ and $2R$ respectively. Shell A carries a charge $+Q$ and shell B carries a charge $-2Q$. What is the net electric potential at a distance of $r = 1.5R$ from the common centre?
questions.solution:
The point at $r = 1.5R$ lies outside shell A and inside shell B.

The electric potential due to shell A at this point is:
$V_A = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \dfrac{+Q}{1.5R} = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \dfrac{2Q}{3R}$

The electric potential due to shell B at any point inside it is equal to its surface potential. Thus, the potential due to shell B at $r = 1.5R$ is:
$V_B = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \dfrac{-2Q}{2R} = -\dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \dfrac{Q}{R}$

By the principle of superposition, the net electric potential is:
$V_{net} = V_A + V_B = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \left( \dfrac{2Q}{3R} - \dfrac{Q}{R} \right) = -\dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \dfrac{Q}{3R}$

The incorrect options result from sign errors, assuming the fields cancel, or treating the entire system as a point charge at the centre.

Answer: $-\dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \dfrac{Q}{3R}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): When $N$ identical charged liquid drops coalesce to form a single large drop, the surface charge density of the large drop is strictly greater than that of a single small drop.

Reason (R): During coalescence, the total charge remains conserved while the total surface area of the system increases.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A)
questions.solution:
Assertion (A) is true: Let the radius of a small drop be $r$ and its charge be $q$. Its surface charge density is $\sigma = \dfrac{q}{4\pi r^2}$.
When $N$ drops coalesce, the new radius is $R = N^{1/3}r$ and the new charge is $Q = Nq$.
The new surface charge density is $\sigma' = \dfrac{Q}{4\pi R^2} = \dfrac{Nq}{4\pi (N^{1/3}r)^2} = N^{1/3}\sigma$.
Since $N \gt 1$, we have $\sigma' \gt \sigma$. Thus, the surface charge density increases.

Reason (R) is false: While the total charge is conserved, the total surface area of the system decreases. The initial total surface area is $N(4\pi r^2)$, and the final surface area is $4\pi R^2 = 4\pi (N^{1/3}r)^2 = N^{2/3}(4\pi r^2)$.
Since $N^{2/3} \lt N$ for $N \gt 1$, the total surface area decreases, not increases.

Therefore, (A) is true but (R) is false.

Answer: (A) is true but (R) is false

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two solid conducting spheres of radii $R$ and $2R$ are given charges such that their surface charge densities are equal. The ratio of their electric potentials, $V_1 : V_2$, will be:
questions.solution:
The electric potential at the surface of a conducting sphere is $V = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \dfrac{Q}{r}$.

The charge $Q$ on a sphere can be expressed in terms of its surface charge density $\sigma$ as $Q = \sigma \times 4\pi r^2$.

Substituting this into the potential formula gives:
$V = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \dfrac{\sigma \times 4\pi r^2}{r} = \dfrac{\sigma r}{\varepsilon_0}$

Since the surface charge density $\sigma$ is the same for both spheres, the electric potential is directly proportional to the radius ($V \propto r$).

Therefore, the ratio of their potentials is:
$\dfrac{V_1}{V_2} = \dfrac{R}{2R} = \dfrac{1}{2}$

The ratio is $1 : 2$.

Answer: $1 : 2$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): The electric field at all points inside a uniformly charged hollow conducting sphere is zero.

Reason (R): Any excess charge given to a hollow conducting sphere distributes uniformly throughout its inner volume.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
options: Both Assertion and Reason are true and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion.
Assertion is true but Reason is false.
Assertion is false but Reason is true.
questions.solution:
Assertion (A) is true because the electric field inside a conductor in electrostatic equilibrium is always zero. For a uniformly charged hollow conducting sphere, the field at all internal points ($r \lt R$) is zero.

Reason (R) is false because any excess charge given to a conducting sphere (whether hollow or solid) resides entirely on its outer surface due to mutual repulsion of charges, not throughout its volume. Since the charge resides only on the surface, a Gaussian surface drawn inside encloses no net charge, leading to zero electric field inside.

Answer: Assertion is true but Reason is false.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
A point charge $-q$ (where $q \ll Q$) of mass $m$ is released from rest at a point on the axis of a fixed, uniformly charged ring of radius $R$ and total charge $+Q$. The release point is at a distance of $\sqrt{3}R$ from the centre of the ring. What is the speed of the point charge when it reaches the centre of the ring?
(Assume $\epsilon_0$ is the permittivity of vacuum and neglect gravity)
questions.solution:
Initial potential on the axis of the ring at a distance $x = \sqrt{3}R$ is:

$V_i = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0} \dfrac{Q}{\sqrt{R^2 + x^2}} = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0} \dfrac{Q}{\sqrt{R^2 + 3R^2}} = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0} \dfrac{Q}{2R}$

Initial potential energy of the system is:

$U_i = -qV_i = -\dfrac{Qq}{8\pi\epsilon_0 R}$

Final potential at the centre of the ring ($x = 0$) is:

$V_f = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0} \dfrac{Q}{R}$

Final potential energy of the system is:

$U_f = -qV_f = -\dfrac{Qq}{4\pi\epsilon_0 R}$

Applying conservation of mechanical energy ($K_i + U_i = K_f + U_f$):

$0 - \dfrac{Qq}{8\pi\epsilon_0 R} = \dfrac{1}{2}mv^2 - \dfrac{Qq}{4\pi\epsilon_0 R}$

$\dfrac{1}{2}mv^2 = \dfrac{Qq}{4\pi\epsilon_0 R} - \dfrac{Qq}{8\pi\epsilon_0 R} = \dfrac{Qq}{8\pi\epsilon_0 R}$

$v^2 = \dfrac{Qq}{4\pi\epsilon_0 mR}$

$v = \sqrt{\dfrac{Qq}{4\pi\epsilon_0 mR}}$

Answer: $\sqrt{\dfrac{Qq}{4\pi\epsilon_0 mR}}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two charged conducting spheres A and B are connected by a thin conducting wire. If the ratio of the electric field magnitudes at the surfaces of spheres A and B is $4 : 1$, what is the ratio of their radii $\left(\dfrac{R_A}{R_B}\right)$?
questions.solution:
When two conducting spheres are connected by a wire, charge flows until they reach the same electrostatic potential ($V_A = V_B$).

The electric field magnitude at the surface of a conducting sphere is given by $E = \dfrac{V}{R}$.

Since the potential $V$ is the same for both spheres, the electric field is inversely proportional to the radius ($E \propto \dfrac{1}{R}$).

Therefore, $E_A R_A = E_B R_B \Rightarrow \dfrac{R_A}{R_B} = \dfrac{E_B}{E_A}$.

Given $\dfrac{E_A}{E_B} = 4$, we find $\dfrac{R_A}{R_B} = \dfrac{1}{4}$.

Answer: $1 : 4$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: An electric dipole of dipole moment $\vec{p}$ is placed at the origin and aligned along the x-axis. A test charge $q_0$ is moved from the point $(0, a, 0)$ to the point $(0, b, 0)$. The work done by the electrostatic force during this process is:
questions.solution:
The electric dipole is aligned along the x-axis. The y-z plane represents the equatorial plane of the dipole.

The electric potential at any point on the equatorial plane of a dipole is zero.

The points $(0, a, 0)$ and $(0, b, 0)$ both lie on the y-axis, which is entirely within the equatorial plane.

Thus, the potential at both points is zero ($V_i = 0$ and $V_f = 0$).

The work done by the electrostatic force in moving the test charge $q_0$ is given by $W = -q_0 \Delta V = -q_0 (V_f - V_i) = 0$.

Therefore, the work done is zero.

Answer: Zero

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two isolated conducting spheres of radii $r_1$ and $r_2$ are charged to the same electric potential. The ratio of the charges on the two spheres, $\dfrac{Q_1}{Q_2}$, is:
questions.solution:
The electric potential at the surface of a conducting sphere of radius $r$ and charge $Q$ is given by $V = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \dfrac{Q}{r}$.

Since both spheres are charged to the same potential, we have $V_1 = V_2$.

$\dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \dfrac{Q_1}{r_1} = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \dfrac{Q_2}{r_2}$

Rearranging the terms gives the ratio of their charges:
$\dfrac{Q_1}{Q_2} = \dfrac{r_1}{r_2}$

Answer: $\dfrac{r_1}{r_2}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two parallel infinite line charges having linear charge densities $+\lambda$ and $-\lambda$ are placed at a distance $d$ apart in free space. If the magnitude of the net electric field midway between the two line charges is $E_0$, what is the magnitude of the linear charge density $\lambda$?
questions.solution:
The distance from each line charge to the midpoint is $r = \dfrac{d}{2}$.

The electric field due to the positive line charge at the midpoint is directed towards the negative line charge, with magnitude:
$E_+ = \dfrac{\lambda}{2\pi\epsilon_0 (d/2)} = \dfrac{\lambda}{\pi\epsilon_0 d}$

The electric field due to the negative line charge at the midpoint is also directed towards the negative line charge, with magnitude:
$E_- = \dfrac{\lambda}{2\pi\epsilon_0 (d/2)} = \dfrac{\lambda}{\pi\epsilon_0 d}$

Since both fields point in the same direction, the net electric field $E_0$ is their sum:
$E_0 = E_+ + E_- = \dfrac{\lambda}{\pi\epsilon_0 d} + \dfrac{\lambda}{\pi\epsilon_0 d} = \dfrac{2\lambda}{\pi\epsilon_0 d}$

Rearranging to solve for $\lambda$ gives:
$\lambda = \dfrac{\pi\epsilon_0 d E_0}{2}$

Answer: $\dfrac{\pi\epsilon_0 d E_0}{2}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: For a short electric dipole, what is the ratio of the magnitude of the electric field at a point on its axial line to the magnitude of the electric field at a point on its equatorial line, given that both points are at the same large distance $r$ from the centre of the dipole?
questions.solution:
The magnitude of the electric field at a point on the axial line of a short electric dipole at a distance $r$ from its centre is given by:

$E_{\text{axial}} = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0} \dfrac{2p}{r^3}$

The magnitude of the electric field at a point on the equatorial line of the same short dipole at the same distance $r$ is given by:

$E_{\text{equatorial}} = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0} \dfrac{p}{r^3}$

Taking the ratio of the two magnitudes:

$\dfrac{E_{\text{axial}}}{E_{\text{equatorial}}} = \dfrac{\dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0} \dfrac{2p}{r^3}}{\dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0} \dfrac{p}{r^3}} = \dfrac{2}{1}$

Therefore, the required ratio is $2:1$.

Answer: $2:1$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two infinitely long parallel wires are separated by a distance $r$ in free space. One wire carries a uniform linear charge density $+\lambda$ and the other carries a uniform linear charge density $-\lambda$. What is the magnitude of the electrostatic force per unit length experienced by either of the wires?
questions.solution:
The electric field produced by the first wire (with charge density $+\lambda$) at the location of the second wire (at distance $r$) is given by:

$E = \dfrac{\lambda}{2\pi\epsilon_0 r}$

Let us consider a segment of length $L$ of the second wire. The charge on this segment is $q = \lambda L$.

The magnitude of the electrostatic force experienced by this segment due to the electric field of the first wire is:

$F = qE = (\lambda L) \left(\dfrac{\lambda}{2\pi\epsilon_0 r}\right)$

Therefore, the magnitude of the force per unit length is:

$\dfrac{F}{L} = \dfrac{\lambda^2}{2\pi\epsilon_0 r}$

Answer: $\dfrac{\lambda^2}{2\pi\epsilon_0 r}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Several solid conducting spheres of different radii are all connected to a common high-voltage generator such that they acquire the same electrostatic potential. Which of the following curves best represents the variation of surface charge density ($\sigma$) of the spheres with their radius ($r$)?
options: A straight line passing through the origin
A horizontal straight line parallel to the $r$-axis
questions.solution:
When the conducting spheres are connected to a common high-voltage generator, they all acquire the same electrostatic potential $V$.

The electric potential at the surface of a conducting sphere of radius $r$ and charge $q$ is given by:
$V = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0} \dfrac{q}{r}$

The surface charge density $\sigma$ is the charge per unit area:
$\sigma = \dfrac{q}{4\pi r^2} \Rightarrow q = \sigma (4\pi r^2)$

Substituting $q$ into the potential equation:
$V = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0} \dfrac{\sigma (4\pi r^2)}{r} = \dfrac{\sigma r}{\epsilon_0}$

Rearranging for surface charge density:
$\sigma = \dfrac{\epsilon_0 V}{r}$

Since the potential $V$ is constant for all spheres, the surface charge density is inversely proportional to the radius ($\sigma \propto \dfrac{1}{r}$).

A graph of a quantity that is inversely proportional to another is a rectangular hyperbola.

Answer: A rectangular hyperbola

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
A solid uncharged conducting sphere contains a spherical cavity. A point charge $+Q$ is placed off-center inside this cavity. Consider the following four statements:
(I) The induced charge on the inner surface of the cavity is $-Q$ and is distributed uniformly.
(II) The induced charge on the outer surface of the sphere is $+Q$ and is distributed uniformly.
(III) The net electric field inside the solid bulk of the conductor is zero.
(IV) The electric field outside the sphere is radially outward and spherically symmetric.

How many of the given statements are correct?
questions.solution:
The point charge $+Q$ is placed off-center inside the spherical cavity. To maintain a zero electric field inside the solid bulk of the conductor (Statement III is correct), the induced charge $-Q$ on the inner surface of the cavity must distribute non-uniformly to cancel the asymmetric field of the off-center charge (Statement I is incorrect).

The isolated conducting sphere is initially uncharged, so a net charge of $+Q$ is induced on its outer surface. Since the outer surface is perfectly spherical and there is no external electric field, this charge $+Q$ distributes uniformly over the outer surface (Statement II is correct).

Because the charge distribution on the outer surface is uniform and spherical, the electric field outside the sphere behaves as if a point charge $+Q$ is situated at the center of the sphere. Thus, it is radially outward and spherically symmetric (Statement IV is correct).

Therefore, exactly 3 statements are correct.

Answer: 3

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two point charges $+2 \mu\text{C}$ and $-2 \mu\text{C}$ are placed at the coordinates $(0, 2\text{ cm}, 0)$ and $(0, -2\text{ cm}, 0)$ respectively. If this electric dipole is placed in a uniform electric field $\vec{E} = 5 \times 10^5 \hat{i}\text{ N C}^{-1}$, what is the torque vector experienced by the dipole?
questions.solution:
The electric dipole moment $\vec{p}$ is a vector directed from the negative charge to the positive charge.

Position of $-q$ is $(0, -2\text{ cm}, 0)$ and position of $+q$ is $(0, 2\text{ cm}, 0)$.
The displacement vector $\vec{d}$ from $-q$ to $+q$ is:
$\vec{d} = (2 - (-2))\hat{j}\text{ cm} = 4\hat{j}\text{ cm} = 0.04\hat{j}\text{ m}$

The dipole moment $\vec{p}$ is:
$\vec{p} = q\vec{d} = (2 \times 10^{-6}\text{ C}) \times (0.04\hat{j}\text{ m}) = 8 \times 10^{-8}\hat{j}\text{ C m}$

The electric field is given as $\vec{E} = 5 \times 10^5 \hat{i}\text{ N C}^{-1}$.

The torque $\vec{\tau}$ experienced by the dipole is the cross product of $\vec{p}$ and $\vec{E}$:
$\vec{\tau} = \vec{p} \times \vec{E}$
$\vec{\tau} = (8 \times 10^{-8}\hat{j}) \times (5 \times 10^5 \hat{i})$
$\vec{\tau} = (8 \times 5 \times 10^{-3}) (\hat{j} \times \hat{i})$
$\vec{\tau} = 40 \times 10^{-3} (-\hat{k})\text{ N m}$
$\vec{\tau} = -0.04 \hat{k}\text{ N m}$

Answer: $-0.04 \hat{k}\text{ N m}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): For a uniformly charged solid conducting sphere of radius $R$, the electric field at a distance $r$ ($r \gt R$) from the center is given by $\dfrac{VR}{r^2}$, where $V$ is the potential on the surface.

Reason (R): The electric potential at a distance $r \gt R$ from the center is given by $V(r) = V\left(\dfrac{R^2}{r^2}\right)$, and the electric field is the negative gradient of the potential.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
options: Both Assertion and Reason are true and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion.
Assertion is true but Reason is false.
Assertion is false but Reason is true.
questions.solution:
Assertion is true: The potential on the surface of the conducting sphere is $V = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{q}{R}$. The electric field outside the sphere at distance $r \gt R$ is $E = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{q}{r^2}$. Substituting $q = 4\pi\varepsilon_0 V R$ into the electric field expression gives $E = \dfrac{V R}{r^2}$.

Reason is false: The electric potential outside the sphere at a distance $r \gt R$ is $V(r) = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{q}{r}$. In terms of surface potential $V$, this is $V(r) = V\left(\dfrac{R}{r}\right)$, not $V\left(\dfrac{R^2}{r^2}\right)$. The electric field is indeed the negative gradient of the potential ($E = -\dfrac{dV}{dr}$), but the expression for $V(r)$ given in the reason is incorrect.

Answer: Assertion is true but Reason is false.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The electric field $E$ due to a charged spherical object of radius $R$ is found to be zero for $r \lt  R$ and proportional to $\dfrac{1}{r^2}$ for $r \gt  R$ (where $r$ is the distance from the centre of the object). Which of the following objects could produce this electric field profile?
options: A uniformly charged solid non-conducting sphere only
A uniformly charged hollow conducting sphere only
A uniformly charged solid conducting sphere only
Either a uniformly charged solid conducting sphere or a uniformly charged hollow conducting sphere
questions.solution:
For $r \lt R$, the electric field is zero. This indicates that there is no charge enclosed within any radius $r \lt R$.

For $r \gt R$, the electric field is proportional to $\dfrac{1}{r^2}$, which is characteristic of a spherical charge distribution where the entire charge can be assumed to be concentrated at the centre.

In both a hollow conducting sphere and a solid conducting sphere, any excess charge resides entirely on the outer surface. Therefore, the electric field inside ($r \lt R$) is zero, and outside ($r \gt R$) it follows the inverse-square law.

In contrast, a uniformly charged solid non-conducting sphere has charge distributed throughout its volume, so its internal electric field is non-zero and proportional to $r$. Thus, the given profile can be produced by either a solid or a hollow conducting sphere.

Answer: Either a uniformly charged solid conducting sphere or a uniformly charged hollow conducting sphere

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two solid spherical conductors, A and B, have radii $R$ and $2R$ respectively. Both spheres have the same uniform surface charge density $\sigma$. Let $E_A$ be the magnitude of the electric field at a distance of $3R$ from the centre of sphere A, and $E_B$ be the magnitude of the electric field at a distance of $4R$ from the centre of sphere B. The ratio $E_A : E_B$ is:
questions.solution:
For a spherical conductor of radius $r_0$ and surface charge density $\sigma$, the total charge is $Q = \sigma (4\pi r_0^2)$.

The electric field at a distance $r$ ($r \ge r_0$) from the centre is given by:
$E = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \dfrac{Q}{r^2} = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \dfrac{\sigma (4\pi r_0^2)}{r^2} = \dfrac{\sigma r_0^2}{\varepsilon_0 r^2}$

For sphere A, radius $r_0 = R$ and distance $r = 3R$:
$E_A = \dfrac{\sigma R^2}{\varepsilon_0 (3R)^2} = \dfrac{\sigma}{9\varepsilon_0}$

For sphere B, radius $r_0 = 2R$ and distance $r = 4R$:
$E_B = \dfrac{\sigma (2R)^2}{\varepsilon_0 (4R)^2} = \dfrac{\sigma (4R^2)}{\varepsilon_0 (16R^2)} = \dfrac{\sigma}{4\varepsilon_0}$

Taking the ratio:
$\dfrac{E_A}{E_B} = \dfrac{\sigma / 9\varepsilon_0}{\sigma / 4\varepsilon_0} = \dfrac{4}{9}$

Answer: $4 : 9$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Four point charges $-Q,-q, 2 q$ and $2 Q$ are placed, one at each corner of the square. The relation between $Q$ and $q$ for which the potential at the centre of the square is zero is
questions.solution: Let $a$ be the side length of the square $A B C D$. $\begin{aligned} & A C=B D=\sqrt{a^2+a^2}=a \sqrt{2} \\ & O A=O B=O C=O D=\frac{a \sqrt{2}}{2}=\frac{a}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}$ Potential is a scalar quantity. Potential at the centre $O$ due to given charge configuration is $\begin{aligned} & V=\frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0}\left[\frac{(-Q)}{\left(\frac{a}{\sqrt{2}}\right)}+\frac{(-q)}{\left(\frac{a}{\sqrt{2}}\right)}+\frac{(2 q)}{\left(\frac{a}{\sqrt{2}}\right)}+\frac{2 Q}{\left(\frac{a}{\sqrt{2}}\right)}\right]=0 \\ & \Rightarrow-Q-q+2 q+2 Q=0 \\ & \text { or } Q+q=0 \text { or } Q=-q\end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A charge particle is moving along electric field as shown in figure. What is horizontal displacement of the charge particle when it descends a distance of $y$ meter? Given $Q / m=9.6 \times 10^7 \mathrm{C} / \mathrm{kg}, E=5 \times 10^5 \mathrm{~V} / \mathrm{m}$, $y=84 \mathrm{~cm}, g=10 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}^2$
questions.solution:
Suppose particle falls down a distance $y$ in time $t$ so
$y=\frac{1}{2} g t^2 ; t=\sqrt{\frac{2 y}{g}}$
Now for $x$-axis
$\begin{aligned} & x=\frac{1}{2} a_x t^2=\frac{1}{2} \cdot \frac{Q E}{m} \cdot \frac{2 y}{g} \\ & =\frac{1}{2} \times \frac{9.6 \times 10^7 \times 5 \times 10^5 \times 2 \times 84 \times 10^{-2}}{10} \\ & =403.2 \times 10^{10} \mathrm{~m}=4.03 \times 10^8 \mathrm{~m}\end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
Assertion : In the absence of an externally applied electric field, the displacement per unit volume of a polar dielectric material is always zero.
Reason : In polar dielectrics, each molecule has a permanent dipole moment but these are randomly oriented in the absence of an externally applied electric field.
options: If both assertion and reason are true and reason is the correct explanation of assertion.
If both assertion and reason are true but reason is not the correct explanation of assertion.
If assertion is true but reason is false.
If both assertion and reason are false.
questions.solution: No Solution Available

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A long solid non-conducting cylinder of radius $R$ is charged such that the volume charge density is proportional to $r$ where $r$ is the distance from axis. The electric field $E$ at a distance $r(r \lt  R)$ will depend on $r$ as
questions.solution: $\begin{aligned} & (\mathbf{b}): \rho \propto r ; \rho=K r \\ & d Q=\rho V \\ & \quad=K r(2 \pi r d r) \times l\end{aligned}$ Using Gauss's Law, $\begin{aligned} & E .2 \pi r l=\frac{\int_0^r K r .2 \pi r l . d r}{\varepsilon_0} \\ & \Rightarrow E=K \frac{r^2}{3 \varepsilon_0} \\ & \therefore E \propto r^2\end{aligned}$

Potential at the surface of the sphere, $V_s=k \frac{Q}{R}$
Potential at the centre of the sphere, $V_c=\frac{3}{2} k \frac{Q}{R}$

Let $v_0=$ speed of the particle at the centre of the sphere.
$\begin{aligned} & \frac{1}{2} m v^2=-q\left[V_{\infty}-V_s\right]=q k \frac{Q}{R} \\ & \frac{1}{2} m v_0^2=-q\left[V_{\infty}-V_c\right]=q \cdot \frac{3}{2} k \frac{Q}{R}\end{aligned}$
Dividing eqn. (ii) by eqn. (i),

questions.solution: Consider an electric dipole with $-q$ charge at $A$ and $+q$ charge at $B$, placed along $z$-axis, such that its dipole moment is in negative $z$ direction. i.e., $p_{\mathrm{z}}=-10^{-7} \mathrm{Cm}$ The electric field is along positive direction of $z$-axis, such that $\frac{d E}{d z}=10^5 \mathrm{NC}^{-1} \mathrm{~m}^{-1}$ From, $F=q d E=(q \times d z) \times \frac{d E}{d z}=p \frac{d E}{d z}$ Force experienced by the system in the negative $z$-direction, $F=-p \times\left(-\frac{d E}{d z}\right)=10^{-7} \times\left(-10^5\right)=-10^{-2} \mathrm{~N}$

questions.q: If same charge $q$ is placed inside a sphere and cube having radius 1 m and side 2 m respectively. What will be the ratio of flux passing through them?

questions.q: A certain charge $Q$ is divided into two parts $q$ and $Q-q$. How the charge $Q$ and $q$ must be related so that when $q$ and $(Q-q)$ is placed at a certain distance apart experience maximum electrostatic repulsion?
questions.solution:
The electrostatic force of repulsion between the charge $q$ and $(Q-q)$ at separation $r$ is given by
$F=\frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} \frac{q(Q-q)}{r^2}=\frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} \frac{q Q-q^2}{r^2}$
If $F$ is maximum, then $\partial F / \partial q=0$ i.e. $\frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} \cdot \frac{(Q-2 q)}{r^2}=0$
As $\frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0 r^2}$ is constant, therefore
$Q-2 q=0$ or $Q=2 q$

questions.solution:
At closest distance $r$ its whole KE is converted into PE
$\therefore \frac{1}{2} m v^2=\frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} \frac{Q \cdot q}{r} \Rightarrow r=\frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} \frac{Q \cdot q}{m v^2}$

questions.q: Two identical conducting balls $A$ and $B$ have positive charges $q_1$ and $q_2$ respectively. But $q_1 \neq q_2$. The balls are brought together so that they touch each other and then kept in their original positions. The force between them is

greater than that before the balls touched
same as that before the balls touched
questions.solution: According to coulomb's law, the force of repulsion between them is given by $F=\frac{q_1 q_2}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0 r^2}$ When the charged spheres $A$ and $B$ are brought in contact, each sphere will attain equal charge $q^{\prime}q^{\prime}=\frac{q_1+q_2}{2}$ Now, the force of repulsion between them at the same distance $r$ is $F^{\prime}=\frac{q^{\prime} \times q^{\prime}}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0 r^2}=\frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} \frac{\left(\frac{q_1+q_2}{2}\right)\left(\frac{q_1+q_2}{2}\right)}{r^2}=\frac{\left(\frac{q_1+q_2}{2}\right)^2}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0 r^2}\operatorname{As}\left(\frac{q_1+q_2}{2}\right)^2 \gt q_1 q_2\therefore F^{\prime} \gt F$

questions.q: If the electric flux entering and leaving an enclosed surface respectively are $\phi$, and $\phi_2$, the electric charge inside the surface will be
questions.solution:
According to Gauss theorem "the net electric flux through any closed surface is equal to the net charge inside the surface divided by $\varepsilon_0{ }^{\prime \prime}$.
Therefore, $\quad \phi \propto \frac{q}{\varepsilon_0}$
Let $-q_1$ be the charge, due to which flux $\phi_1$ is entering the surface,
$\phi_1=\frac{-q_1}{\varepsilon_0}-q_1=\varepsilon_0 \phi_1$
Let $+q_2$ be the charge, due to which flux $\phi_2$ is entering the surface.
$\phi_2=\frac{q_2}{\varepsilon_0}$
or $\quad q_2=\varepsilon_0 \phi_2$
So, electric charge inside the surface
$=q_2-q_1\begin{aligned} & =\varepsilon_0 \phi_2+\varepsilon_0 \phi_1 \\ & \Rightarrow \quad=\varepsilon_0\left(\phi_2+\phi_1\right) \end{aligned}$

questions.q: Two spherical conductors $B$ and $C$ having equal radii and carrying equal charges in them repel each other with a force $F$ when kept apart at some distance. A third spherical conductor having same radius as that of $B$ but uncharged, is brought in contact with $B$, then brought in contact with $C$ and finally removed away from both. The new force of repulsion between $B$ and $C$ is
questions.solution:
Let the spherical conductors $B$ and $C$ have same charge as $q$. The electric force between them is
$F=\frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} \frac{q^2}{r^2}r$, being the distance between them.
When third uncharged conductor $A$ is brought in contact with $B$, then charge on each conductor
$q_A=q_B=\frac{q_A+q_B}{2}=\frac{0+q}{2}=\frac{q}{2}$
When this conductor $A$ is now brought in contact with $C$, then charge on each conductor
$q_A=q_C=\frac{q_A+q_C}{2}=\frac{(q / 2)+q}{2}=\frac{3 q}{4}$
Hence, electric force acting between $B$ and $C$ is
$\begin{aligned}
F^{\prime}=\frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} \frac{q_B q_C}{r^2} & =\frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} \frac{(q / 2)(3 q / 4)}{r^2} \\
& =\frac{3}{8}\left[\frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} \frac{q^2}{r^2}\right]=\frac{3 F}{8}
\end{aligned}$

questions.q: Two similar charges having mass $m$ and $2 m$ are placed in an electric field. The ratio of their kinetic energy is :

Force on charged particle is electric field
$F=q E\therefore$ Acceleration $a=\frac{F}{m}=\frac{q E}{m}\therefore$ Velocity
$\begin{aligned} v & =u+a t \\ & =0+\frac{q E}{m} t\end{aligned}$
So, kinetic energy
$\begin{aligned} & =\frac{\frac{1}{2} m_1\left(\frac{q E}{m_1} t\right)^2}{\frac{1}{2} m_2\left(\frac{q E}{m_2} t\right)^2} \\ & =\frac{m_2}{m_1}=\frac{2 m}{m} \\ & =\frac{2}{1} \\ & =2: 1\end{aligned}$

questions.q: If an insulated non-conducting sphere of radius $R$ has charge density $\rho$. The electric field at a distance $r$ from the centre of sphere $(r \gt R)$ will be
questions.solution:
Charge which is enclosed in the surface is given by $\quad \sigma=\frac{4}{3} \pi r^3 \rho$
Now according to Gaussian law
$\begin{aligned} \varepsilon \phi E d s & =\sigma, \varepsilon_0 E 4 \pi r^2=\frac{4}{3} \pi r^3 \rho \\ E & =\frac{\rho r}{3 \varepsilon_0}\end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A charged particle is suspended in equilibrium in a uniform vertical electric field of intensity $20000 \mathrm{~V} / \mathrm{m}$. If mass of the particle is $9.6 \times 10^{-16} \mathrm{~kg}$, the charge on it and excess number of electrons on the-particle respectively are $\left(\mathrm{g}=10 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}^2\right)$
questions.solution:
Charge on the particle is given by
$\begin{aligned}q E & =m g \text { or } q=\frac{m g}{E} \\& =\frac{9.6 \times 10^{-16} \times 10}{20000}=4.8 \times 10^{-19}
\end{aligned}$
When there is an excess of $n$ electrons on the particle, then
$q=n e$
So,
$n=\frac{q}{e}=\frac{4.8 \times 10^{-19}}{1.6 \times 10^{-19}}=3$

The ratio of electrostatic and gravitational forces acting between electron and proton separated by a distance $5 \times 10^{11} \mathrm{~m}$, will be
(Charge on electron $=1.6 \times 10^{-19} \mathrm{C}$, mass of electron $=9.1 \times 10^{-31} \mathrm{~kg}$, mass of proton $=1.6 \times 10^{-27} \mathrm{~kg}$, $\left.G=6.7 \times 10^{-11} \quad \mathrm{Nm}^2 / \mathrm{kg}^2\right)$
questions.solution:
Gravitational force $F=\frac{G M_1 M_2}{r^2}F_G=\frac{6.7 \times 10^{-11} \times 9.1 \times 10^{-31} \times 1.6 \times 10^{-27}}{\left(5 \times 10^{-11}\right)^2}=3.9 \times 10^{-47} \mathrm{~N}$
Electrostatic force $F_E=\frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} \frac{q_1 q_2}{r^2}F_e=\frac{9 \times 10^9 \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19}}{\left(5 \times 10^{-11}\right)^2}=9.22 \times 10^{-8} \mathrm{~N}\therefore \quad \frac{\text { Electrostatic force }}{\text { Gravitational force }}=\frac{F_E}{F_G}\begin{aligned} & =\frac{9.22 \times 10^{-8}}{3.9 \times 10^{-47}} \\ & =2.36 \times 10^{39}\end{aligned}$
